slices.label: White Southerners

slices.label: Black Southerners

applied.label: Black Men Barred in the South

assumptions: Black men in the former Confederate states cast no votes; the votes they cast in 1868 are removed and nobody takes their place. White voters behave as observed.
howIGotThis: What changed: Black men in the former Confederate states are kept from the polls, as if the Reconstruction Acts had not given them the vote.
I built this change from your words. It is exploratory, not part of the plan fixed before any run.

What historians found (12 findings, strong evidence): Evidence on keeping Black men from the polls comes mainly from 1868 Louisiana and Georgia, where terror suppressed the Republican vote and flipped both states to Seymour. Nationally, the Black vote probably decided the election. Protected Black turnout was very high, at 85-90 percent.
The numbers: the 1860 and 1870 census counts interpolated to 1868 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1868 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

findings.claim: About 700,000 Black people, mostly former slaves, registered to vote under the Reconstruction framework; Texas, Mississippi and Virginia were not yet readmitted by 1868.

findings.claim: Where protected, Black turnout was very high: over 85% of registered Black voters in South Carolina in 1867, and about 88% in Virginia (93,145 of 105,832).

findings.claim: South Carolina whites boycotted the 1867 convention vote: only 2,350 whites voted for it, so about 95% of eligible whites voted against or stayed home.
